list_description: "A recent reanalysis by Anne G. E. Collins (<a href='https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02340-0'>2025</a>) suggests that learning in the RLWM paradigm may be driven more by Habit (H) and Working Memory (WM) than by a slow reinforcement learning (RL) process. In this project, I used the custom <code>multiRL</code> R package to re-implement these models, starting from simple models (RL, WM, H) and gradually building more complex combinations to evaluate parameter recovery and parameter redundancy. The results showed that a simple 3-parameter HWM model was enough to recover the main experimental effects, while adding more parameters often reduced model performance, consistent with Occam’s razor. In addition, although different estimation methods performed reasonably well for simple models, only simulation-based inference (SBI) methods maintained good parameter recovery as model complexity increased, with ABC showing the strongest overall performance."
responsibilities: "Stand-Up Comedy."

Our goal in model building was to develop a model with recoverable parameters (indicating good reliability) that could also reproduce the three experimental effects shown below (indicating good validity).

1. If a parameter isn’t recoverable, it suggests it may be redundant or effectively masked by other parameters.
2. If a model cannot even reproduce the experimental effects—oh come on, then there is really no point in discussing it further.

Here is my personal interpretation of Collins ([2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02340-0)). In an MDP, two systems are involved: a reinforcement learning system and a working memory system. Within the reinforcement learning system, the process can be further differentiated into standard RL and Habit (H) based on whether the feedback is constantly treated as a subjective value of 1. The WM system consists of three parameters: the memory decay rate(`zeta`), working memory `capacity`, and the mixture `weight` between the RL and WM systems. Additionally, there are two system-independent parameters: sticky choice (action perseveration) and lapse rate (the probability of making an accidental motor error). 

::: {style="text-align: center;"}

HWM model remade using `multiRL` (originally proposed by Collins ([2025](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02340-0))) did not show good parameter recovery (in fact, the parameter recovery results reported in the original paper were also relatively weak for several parameters). It also failed to reproduce the experimental effects observed in human participants. 

::: {style="text-align: center;"}

Compared to the full six-parameter HWM model, the simplified HWM model without the `weight`, `lapse`, and `sticky` parameters was already able to reproduce the main experimental effects reasonably well. In addition, it showed substantially better parameter recovery performance.
